title: The Musk Deer
hookLine: a deer hunts the whole forest for a scent it carries
carry: Ram lives in every heart, mine too
tomorrow: Why does a holy poem begin with a bow?

cards: A deer moves through the forest, head low, nose working. There's a scent in the air, rich and sweet, and it's maddening, because it's everywhere and nowhere. The deer checks behind a tree.
Under a bush. Down by the stream. The scent is just as strong in each place, and never any closer.
It keeps searching until it's worn out. Kabir put this deer in two lines. It's the third doha this week, and the last day with the weaver of Kashi.

teach.h: THE MUSK IS IN THE DEER.
teach.b: The doha begins, in Hindi, kasturi kundal basai. Kasturi is musk, the prized scent. Roughly: the musk lives in the deer's own navel, and the deer goes searching for it through the forest.
Then the second line: just so, Ram is in every body, every heart, and the world doesn't see. Every place smelled of musk because the deer brought it to every place.
This is one of Hinduism's great teachings: God isn't only far away, in a temple or a heaven.

God dwells within. In Hindi, God is often called antaryami, the one who lives inside and knows the heart. Kabir's Ram, the name his teacher cried out on the steps at Kashi, isn't held in one temple or one image.
Put the three dohas together. Go looking for the bad one, and you end up searching your own heart. Read book after book, and the lesson is still two and a half letters, love.

Search the whole forest for God, and the scent was in you all along. Kabir's life ends, tradition says, with one more turn. When he died, his followers, Hindus and Muslims, each wanted to give him their own last rites.
When they lifted the sheet, there was no body, only a heap of flowers. So each group took half, and honored him in its own way.
Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs, whose scripture keeps his verses, still honor him today: one saint, remembered by different paths with different rites.

how: The musk deer doha is quoted as a saying about looking for God far away; quietly repeating a name of God, like Ram, is a common Hindu practice; and the story of the flowers under Kabir's sheet is told by people of more than one community who honor him.

o: the weaver-poet who said Ram is in every heart
the deer that searched the forest for musk
a king who built temples to Ram across Kashi

games.q: Kabir's three dohas — tap the pairs.
p: reads two and a half letters

s: in the doha, the deer finds the musk behind a tree
it searches the forest, but the musk is in its own navel.
Kabir's Ram, in this doha, is in every heart
the world doesn't see, the second line says.
tradition says Kabir's followers found his body and buried it
under the sheet they found only flowers, and each group took half.

games.q: you're the deer in Kabir's doha. a sweet scent is everywhere, and never any closer. what does the doha say you do?
o: search the whole forest for it.
follow the stream out of the forest.
games.why: the deer searches the forest, but the musk is in its own navel. Kabir says Ram is in every heart, and the world doesn't see.

practice: Sit still and, on each breath out, silently say a name of God: Ram, the name Kabir took on the steps, or the one your family uses.

When your mind runs off into the forest, after a plan or a worry, notice it the way you'd notice the deer, and come back to the name, already here inside. If you don't pray, rest on the words already here instead.

wordCard.voice: Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: the musk is in the deer's own navel, and it searches the forest; Ram is in every heart, and the world doesn't see.

orig.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: musk, the scent the deer searches for in today's doha.

carryVoice: Your line: Ram lives in every heart, mine too. The musk was in the deer all along. That's day nine hundred twenty-three.
